column7: hadd: h(s) = sum of costs achieving each part of overall goal independently. Good amount faster than others but may overestimate costs and not admissible.
hmax: h(s) = max(cost of each part of overall goal independently). IS THE SLOWEST, but solid guidance and admissible. Can underestimate.
hsa: hadd except sets of facts are remembered instead of independent parts of overall goal. More accurate than hadd, faster than hmax, but still not admissible.
hff: relaxed plan where h(s) = #actions in relaxed plan. Good guidance but plan extraction + compute costs is bad plus still not admissible.
blind: 0 is returned for every state, literally no heuristic info besides brute force. No computational cost but explores huge parts of search space. Relatively fast.
lmcut: Repeatedly identifies landmarks to be achieved by any real plan and finds cuts (sets of actions) to achieve them. Adds min action cost for each cut, and IS ADMISSIBLE. Relatively fast.
landmark: Landmarks MUST BE TRUE at some point in ALL valid plans. Strong heuristic, not admissible.

Pyperplan: Pure Python, which is SLOW. Basic searches include wastar, astar, gbf, bfs, ehs, ids, sat. DEFAULT THAT WAS USED IS wastar. Since the main task was to evaluate heuristics, I cared less about traversing or grid searching these.

Pyperplan-opt: Optimized Pyperplan w/ astar, bfs, ids searches, default being astar. OPTIMIZED data structures & BETTER PRUNING. For this task, not much difference between pyperplan and pyperplan-opt.
fast-downward: HIGHLY OPTIMIZED C++ planner. REALLY fast due to C++ and also optimized algorithms (e.g. search engines, preferred operators, etc.)
